source.title: Practical Scaling Laws: Converting Compute into Performance in a Data-Constrained World

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some tables are flattened in the supplied text, but the main results and relevant aggregate findings are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study proposes and evaluates a refinement of established scaling laws, arguing that the usual power-law-plus-constant form has structural limits in data-constrained and multi-epoch settings. It tests extrapolation on new experiments and published grids.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own scaling experiments, held-out prediction comparisons, allocation analysis, and fitting-dependence findings. Claims and results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows. Downstream-task performance is explicitly out of scope.
record.test_reason: The study argues the Chinchilla power-law-plus-constant form needs restating outside data-rich single-epoch training. It measures extrapolation error of power-law-based forms, including plain Chinchilla, on four new multi-epoch grids and five published LLM grids. These results bear on V2, V5 and V7. Its V3 content is derivation and an illustrative calculation, not measurement.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim the form reduces to Chinchilla in the data-rich single-epoch limit. They claim it wins 16 of 18 high-C/high-D extrapolation cells, with state-of-the-art RMSE on every published LLM grid, and that it can serve as a general-purpose LLM scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: This study proposes a new three-axis saturating form and refits prior scaling-law datasets; it does not reproduce the original Kaplan or Hoffmann measurement protocol. Its own grids include multi-epoch exposure and data-constrained settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that fitted constants can shift with parameter-counting convention, architecture family, and training recipe. The outcome also varies by holdout condition: the proposed form underperforms on TinyStories high-C and MNIST high-D. Fit behavior depends on whether the grid identifies separate N, D, and T effects; the Chinchilla-style T = D grid weakly identifies overfitting parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: A cost-aware allocation in which the optimum shifts toward smaller D, more epochs and a smaller N as the data-to-compute price ratio η grows. It is illustrated with invented overfitting constants.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: When unique data has a price, loss-optimal allocation trades unique data for repeated epochs.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed unique data, the derived compute-optimal model size saturates at a finite value.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under a data constraint, compute-optimal model size stops growing with compute.

record.problems: The paper's internal CIFAR-100, Darcy, and TinyStories grids use a single seed per cell. Some source grids average replicated cells with spreads of 0.17 to 0.36 nats. The Gadre grid is small, with only 4 cells held out under each protocol. Several allocation results are illustrative or derived from the proposed form rather than empirical tests of compute-optimal trends. The authors also note weak identification of overfitting parameters on grids without varied-N small-D or multi-epoch conditions.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-form RMSE values for every dataset and holdout, the full bootstrap intervals, ablation tables, and all fitted-parameter entries are not transcribed as separate rows; the record keeps the study's aggregate extrapolation finding, explicitly named exceptions, and findings directly relevant to the claim. See Tables 2–3 and 5, and Appendix I.1/Table 9.

untested.parts: No clean estimate of parameter, token or compute power-law exponents for language-model pretraining with the other axes non-bottlenecking. The LLM grids are refits of published data.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude. Holdouts are the top ~10% of C or D, and the far benchmark is only 1.7–5.4× in compute.
No empirical compute-optimal sweep. Allocation results are derived or illustrative.
Entire version; no shape variation at fixed N.
Video, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested.
Entire version; downstream tasks are out of scope.

missing.what: Absolute held-out RMSE of the plain Chinchilla form on each grid. High-C: MNIST 0.331, CIFAR 0.156, Darcy 0.322, TinyStories 0.167; Chinchilla 0.023, Muennighoff 0.093, Gadre 0.037, Porian 0.098, Farseer 0.022.
Ablation in which removing the overfitting term sharply raises extrapolation error on internal grids (e.g. MNIST high-C 0.867 vs 0.127, high-D 1.272 vs 0.137), with little effect on LLM grids.
Absolute far-compute RMSE: ours 0.004, Farseer 0.005, Chinchilla 0.029 (overestimates loss).

record.verdict_notes: R1 is unlinked from V1. MNIST is not language-model pretraining, and its overfitting occurs when data is the bottleneck, so it lies outside V1's premise. The V1 limits_scope label is dropped. V3 labels are dropped: R7–R9 are derivations or illustrations, not measurements. The V5 label is changed from challenges to limits_scope, since power-law terms still fit once saturation and overfitting terms are added. Internal grids other than MNIST use a single seed. The Gadre grid holds out only 4 cells.

versions.untested_parts: Does not independently test clean parameter-, token-, and compute-axis power-law exponents across several orders of magnitude with the other axes demonstrably non-bottlenecking.
The study evaluates specified high-compute and high-data holdouts; it does not establish predictability for every larger-run regime or training setup.

The allocation results are derived from the proposed form and include an illustrative fixed-budget example, rather than an empirical sweep of compute-optimal allocations across budgets and data prices.
No controlled comparison varies depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests selected vision, scientific-ML, and language experiments, including multi-epoch training; does not test video, fine-tuning, transfer, or all other modalities and regimes.
Downstream-task performance is stated to be out of scope.
Does not run controlled experiments varying each fitting or training choice separately to quantify its causal effect on exponents or allocation.

rows.subject: MLP on MNIST
rows.operation_detail: Measured running-min validation loss across parameter, unique-data, and training-exposure sweeps.

conditions.value: 10 seeds per cell; per-cell losses averaged

rows.measure: Running-min validation loss versus FLOPs, parameters, and unique data
rows.value: The reported curves show overfitting with increasing N; for D = 60k, N* appears around 250k. The loss floor descends as D increases.
rows.note: The authors describe the qualitative curves as consistent with their proposed form. This is not a direct estimate of a single power-law exponent.
rows.check: MNIST MLP classification is not language-model pretraining, so it does not bear on V1. The overfitting it shows occurs when data is the bottleneck, which V1 already excludes. For V5 the result is qualitative only: loss falls with D, and non-monotone N appears at fixed D.

rows.subject: Proposed form (Eq. (2)), aggregate across four training experiments and five published LLM grids
rows.operation_detail: Compared held-out high-C and high-D loss predictions against refitted scaling-law forms.

conditions.value: High-C and high-D; approximately 10% of rows, grouped on the held-out axis
MNIST, CIFAR-100, Darcy, TinyStories, Chinchilla, Muennighoff, Gadre, Porian, Farseer

rows.measure: Held-out RMSE in log loss and paired bootstrap comparisons
rows.baseline: Other refitted forms, including Chinchilla, Muennighoff, M4, BNSL, and Farseer
rows.value: Lowest median held-out RMSE in 16 of 18 high-C/high-D cells; ahead of the best competing baseline in those cells by a median factor of 1.5×. Paired-resample wins in those 16 cells were significant at p < 10⁻³.
rows.uncertainty: 200 bootstrap resamples; reported intervals are 2.5%–97.5% quantiles
rows.note: Aggregate across the study's 18 grid-by-holdout cells; the paper states the two exceptions separately.
rows.check: The value is the proposed form's win count against other forms, i.e. the study's own method compared with others. What bears on V2 is the absolute held-out RMSE in Table 2 (e.g. 0.005–0.063 on LLM grids high-C), not the ranking.

source_check.correct: The 16/18 win count compares the proposed method against competing forms; it cannot determine whether V2 or V5 is observed. State: cannot_determine for this aggregate value. Record absolute extrapolation errors and structural failures separately.
source_check.problem: Method-comparison wins are incorrectly recorded as observation of the linked phenomena.

rows.subject: Proposed form (Eq. (2))
rows.operation_detail: Predicted held-out loss for the high-C holdout and compared RMSE with other forms.
rows.value: The proposed form underperformed a baseline.
rows.note: One of the two cells the authors identify as exceptions to the proposed form's lower-RMSE result.
rows.check: Losing to another power-law form is not a failure of extrapolation. On TinyStories high-C the Muennighoff form reaches 0.091 and ours 0.183, so the row cannot show V2 failing. It is a method-vs-method comparison.

rows.subject: Proposed form (Eq. (2))
rows.operation_detail: Predicted held-out loss for the high-D holdout and compared RMSE with other forms.
rows.value: The proposed form underperformed a baseline.
rows.note: One of the two cells the authors identify as exceptions to the proposed form's lower-RMSE result.

rows.size_stated: Five grids: Chinchilla, Muennighoff, Gadre, Porian, and Farseer

rows.subject: Proposed form (Eq. (2))
rows.size_stated: Farseer 400-cell cohort predicting 7 held-out large-model runs
rows.operation_detail: Predicted the Farseer far-compute benchmark runs from the 400-cell cohort.

conditions.value: 7 held-out runs, 1.7 to 5.4× beyond the cohort in compute

rows.value: The proposed form achieved the lowest error and the narrowest interval among the forms compared; the authors state it performed as well as Farseer's own form on this benchmark.
rows.uncertainty: 200 bootstrap resamples; whiskers span the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles
rows.note: The plotted numerical RMSE values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Extrapolation is only 1.7–5.4× in compute, not orders of magnitude. Figure 7 gives RMSE 0.004 (ours), 0.005 (Farseer) and 0.029 (Chinchilla, which overestimates loss).

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine for V2's orders-of-magnitude extrapolation claim. Targets extend 1.7–5.4× beyond calibration compute. Figure 6 confirms the relative ranking and interval width; Figure 7 reports RMSE 0.004 for the proposed form, 0.005 for Farseer and 0.029 for Chinchilla.
source_check.problem: Successful short-range extrapolation and relative ranking do not establish extrapolation orders of magnitude beyond calibration.

rows.subject: Proposed form (Eq. (2)), data-rich asymptotic allocation
rows.operation_detail: Derived the compute-optimal parameter count when unique data is unlimited.
rows.value: N*(C) ∝ C^(β/(α+β)); with Chinchilla-like exponents α ≈ β, N*(C) ∝ C^(1/2).
rows.note: A derivation from the proposed form, not an empirical sweep of optimal allocations.
rows.check: This is an algebraic consequence of a form built to reduce to Chinchilla, not an empirical result on allocation.

rows.subject: Proposed form (Eq. (2)), fixed-unique-data allocation
rows.operation_detail: Derived the compute limit of the optimal model size at fixed unique data.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal parameter count as compute grows
rows.value: The optimal model size approaches a finite value N*∞(D) = (αaDδ/γc)^(1/(α+γ)) rather than growing without bound.
rows.note: This is a result derived from the proposed form, not an empirical measurement.
rows.check: This is a derivation from the proposed form, with no measured compute-optimal sweep. It concerns the fixed-D regime, outside V3's data-unconstrained setting.

rows.subject: Illustrative cost-optimal allocation under the proposed form
rows.operation_detail: Optimized parameter count, unique data, and training duration at fixed total budget for different data-to-compute price ratios.
rows.measure: Cost-optimal N*, D*, T*/D*, and data-dollar share
rows.value: As η increases from 10¹⁰ to 10¹³, D* shrinks from 4.4 × 10⁹ to 8.6 × 10⁸, N* from 5.2 × 10⁹ to 2.1 × 10⁸, T*/D* rises from 2.7 to 1,250, and data-dollar share rises from 12% to 86%.
rows.note: Illustrative calculation using Chinchilla exponents and stated illustrative overfitting constants; it varies data price, not compute budget.
rows.check: This is an illustrative calculation with invented overfitting constants (c, γ, δ) = (2×10³, 0.5, 1.0). It varies the data price, not the compute budget, and is not a measurement.

rows.subject: Proposed form (Eq. (2)), Chinchilla-grid fit
rows.size_stated: 245 rows; N ∈ [5.73 × 10⁷, 1.62 × 10¹⁰] params and D ∈ [2.45 × 10⁸, 3.18 × 10¹¹] tokens
rows.operation_detail: Examined fitted-term contributions and parameter identification on a grid with T = D.
rows.baseline: Undertraining exponent β = 1.295 in the same fit
rows.value: The overfitting term contributes 64% of h at the grid's geometric center, with δ = 0.182 against β = 1.295; the paper says c, γ, and δ are weakly resolved when T and D are coupled.
rows.uncertainty: The paper reports wide marginal confidence intervals for these terms when the fit grid lacks overfitting regimes.
rows.note: The authors state that identifying c, γ, and δ individually requires small-D runs at varied N, multi-epoch runs at varied T/D, or both.
rows.check: This is valid as fit-dependence: on the same Chinchilla grid, the data-axis exponent fitted under this form (β=1.295, δ=0.182) differs sharply from the Chinchilla form's ~0.28. The 'partial' state understates it.

rows.subject: Fitted constants of the proposed form across experiment settings
rows.size_stated: Nine calibration grids across four architecture families and three domains
rows.operation_detail: Compared the scope of fitted constants across settings and identified choices absorbed into the fits.

conditions.value: Architecture family, parameter-counting convention, data distribution, and training recipe

rows.measure: Dependence of fitted scaling-law constants on setup
rows.value: The authors state that fitted constants are not universal and that parameter-counting convention, architecture family, and training recipe can shift them materially.
rows.note: The paper holds recipe choices fixed within each experiment family rather than varying each choice in a controlled comparison.
rows.check: This is the authors' caveat in the Limitations section, not a controlled measurement. The supporting evidence is only the cross-grid spread of fitted constants in Table 5.

relationships.condition: Data-rich single-epoch published LLM grids (Chinchilla, Gadre, Farseer, Porian, Muennighoff) and the Farseer far-compute benchmark
relationships.reason: Power-law-based forms fitted on smaller runs predict held-out larger-C runs with low log-RMSE: ours 0.005–0.063, Chinchilla form 0.022–0.098. Ours reaches 0.004 on far-C (R5, R6, R2). The Chinchilla-form values come from Table 2 text, not the rows.
relationships.display_finding: The proposed form achieved log-RMSE of 0.005–0.063 versus 0.022–0.098 for Chinchilla, reaching 0.004 on the far-compute benchmark.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Data-rich single-epoch published LLM grids (Chinchilla, Gadre, Farseer, Porian, Muennighoff) and the Farseer far-compute benchmark
source_check.reason: The specified group misclassifies Muennighoff: 198/232 cells are multi-epoch, reaching 9000 epochs (Appendix E.2). High-C holds out approximately the largest-compute 10% of rows; Appendix H explicitly extends only 1.7–5.4× beyond calibration compute. Low errors support prediction over these tested ranges, but do not establish V2's orders-of-magnitude extrapolation. The proposed saturating form also does not generally reduce to the original power-law form without additional conditions.

relationships.condition: Multi-epoch data-constrained grids (MNIST, CIFAR-100, Darcy, TinyStories)
relationships.reason: From Table 2 text, not the rows: the plain Chinchilla form's high-C error is 0.331 (MNIST), 0.322 (Darcy), 0.156 (CIFAR), 0.167 (TinyStories). Even the best form reaches only 0.08–0.18, much worse than on LLM grids (R2).
relationships.display_finding: Chinchilla high-compute errors were 0.331 for MNIST, 0.322 for Darcy, 0.156 for CIFAR-100 and 0.167 for TinyStories; even the best form had errors of 0.08–0.18.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Multi-epoch data-constrained grids (MNIST, CIFAR-100, Darcy, TinyStories)
source_check.reason: Table 2 confirms Chinchilla high-C log-RMSE of 0.331, 0.156, 0.322 and 0.167 respectively, qualifying extrapolation reliability in these regimes. These absolute errors should replace R2's method win count as evidence.

relationships.condition: Vision, PDE-surrogate and multi-epoch language settings
relationships.reason: Power-law terms still describe these surfaces, but non-monotone loss in N at fixed D (R1) means the plain form needs saturation and an overfitting term. The ablation shows large error without the overfitting term (MNIST high-C 0.867 vs 0.127; Table 9 text, not the rows). R2 is linked to V5 in the rows but does not itself show the change.
relationships.display_finding: Nonmonotonic model-size dependence required saturation and overfitting terms; removing the overfitting term increased high-compute MNIST error from 0.127 to 0.867.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Vision, PDE-surrogate and multi-epoch language settings
source_check.reason: Figure 2 shows increasing validation loss with excessive model capacity at fixed data; the additive Chinchilla form cannot represent this behavior. Appendix I.1 and Table 9 confirm degradation without the overfitting term, including MNIST high-C 0.867 versus 0.127. These results qualify transfer of the same functional form across regimes.

relationships.condition: Refits across nine grids, including the Chinchilla grid
relationships.reason: Fitted exponents depend on the functional form and grid. On the Chinchilla grid this form gives β=1.295 with an overfitting term supplying 64% of h (R10). The authors state constants shift with counting convention and recipe (R11).
relationships.display_finding: Across nine grids, exponents depended on form and grid; the Chinchilla-grid fit gave β=1.295 with an overfitting term supplying 64% of h, while parameter-accounting conventions and training recipes changed constants.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Refits across nine grids, including the Chinchilla grid
source_check.reason: Appendix C.3 explicitly reports β=1.295 and an overfitting-term contribution of 64% of h on the Chinchilla grid, with weak identification when T=D. Section 6 states that counting convention, architecture and training recipe can materially shift fitted constants. Support concerns fit dependence; those setup choices are not independently manipulated.
